title: Mittelschmerz - Right-Sided Lower Abdominal Pain with Ultrasound Report
patient_instructions: You are Jenna Wallace, a 24-year-old woman with mild pain in the lower right side of your tummy. The pain is mild (about 3/10), settles with paracetamol (Panadol) and rest, and you have had this same kind of pain before in previous months. Your last menstrual period was 14 days ago and your periods are regular. You are sexually active with one partner and use condoms; you have not missed a period. You are very worried about your gallbladder because your mother had surgery for gallstones and you are frightened of having an operation - raise this concern early. If asked: no fever, no vomiting, no heavy or unusual vaginal bleeding, no vaginal discharge, appetite normal, no shift of pain. Ideas: you think it might be your gallbladder. Concerns: you fear needing gallbladder surgery. Expectations: you want to know what the scan means and whether you need an operation. Affect: anxious but calm, reassured by clear explanation. Speak in everyday language.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor at a rural NSW clinic. Jenna Wallace, a 24-year-old woman, presents with right-sided lower abdominal pain. A pelvic/abdominal ultrasound is available: ruptured follicle in the right ovary, free fluid in the pouch of Douglas, incidental gallstones with a normal (non-inflamed, non-thickened) gallbladder, and the appendix not visualised (no prior appendicectomy). Tasks: (1) Briefly clarify the key history. (2) Interpret and explain the ultrasound results in lay language. (3) Give your diagnosis with reasons, address her concern about the gallbladder, and outline management. Assume a negative urine pregnancy test is available.
examiner_instructions: Reward candidates who exclude ectopic pregnancy in a woman of reproductive age (menstrual, sexual and contraceptive history plus a documented negative beta-hCG) before settling on Mittelschmerz, and who keep ovarian torsion and ruptured cyst on the differential. The expected diagnosis is Mittelschmerz (mid-cycle pain from follicular rupture). The hardest task is explaining the ultrasound in plain language: ovulation, follicle rupture, mid-cycle timing, free fluid, and why the gallstones (normal gallbladder) and non-visualised appendix are not the cause. Check the candidate addresses the gallbladder concern with specific reasons and provides Australian-standard safety-netting. Prompt if needed: 'How will you exclude pregnancy?' Use consistent female patient naming.

criteria: Confirms haemodynamic stability and explores the pain (mild, recurrent, relieved by rest/paracetamol)
Takes menstrual, sexual and contraceptive history; LMP 14 days ago
Actively excludes ectopic pregnancy (asks about missed periods, requests beta-hCG)
Addresses the patient's stated gallbladder concern within the history
Diagnoses Mittelschmerz with reasons (mid-cycle timing, recurrent, mild, relieved by rest)
Correctly interprets the ultrasound (ruptured follicle + fluid in pouch of Douglas) and dismisses incidental gallstones and non-visualised appendix
Retains ovarian torsion, ruptured cyst and appendicitis as differentials
Conservative management: simple analgesia (paracetamol or NSAID), rest, heat pack, reassurance
Provides clear safety-net red flags with an urgent-review threshold
Mentions ovulation-suppressing COCP as an option for recurrent troublesome cases (with caveat)
Explains ultrasound and diagnosis in clear lay language and checks understanding
Empathically reassures about the gallbladder with specific reasons

red_flags: Ectopic pregnancy must be actively excluded in any woman of reproductive age with lower abdominal pain - document a negative beta-hCG
Ovarian torsion (sudden severe unilateral pain, vomiting, adnexal mass/tenderness) is a time-critical surgical emergency mimic
Severe worsening pain, fainting/dizziness, fever or heavy vaginal bleeding warrants immediate ED presentation
Do not accept a benign diagnosis on the basis of LMP timing alone without excluding pregnancy
australian_guidelines: Murtagh / RACGP: Mittelschmerz (ruptured Graafian follicle) is managed with explanation and reassurance, simple analgesics (paracetamol) and heat-pack comfort
eTG / RACGP: exclude ectopic pregnancy with beta-hCG in reproductive-age women presenting with lower abdominal pain
Australian prescribing convention: use generic drug names first - paracetamol (brand Panadol), ibuprofen (brand Nurofen); avoid listing a drug and its brand as if separate agents
Ovulation suppression with the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) may prevent recurrent Mittelschmerz - acute-episode management is what the exam asks for; call 000 for collapse
learning_objectives: Exclude pregnancy and time-critical gynaecological emergencies before diagnosing benign mid-cycle pain
Interpret and explain an ultrasound report to a patient in plain language
Deliver reassurance with specific evidence when a patient fixates on an incidental finding
Provide Australian-standard conservative management and safety-netting for Mittelschmerz
key_points: Mittelschmerz is mid-cycle (around day 14) pain from follicular enlargement/rupture with peritoneal irritation from blood and follicular fluid
Fluid in the pouch of Douglas plus a ruptured right ovarian follicle fits the diagnosis; incidental gallstones with a normal gallbladder do not
50-85% of normal appendices are not visualised on ultrasound - non-visualisation does not imply appendicitis
Always exclude ectopic pregnancy and ovarian torsion before reassuring

citations.claim: Mittelschmerz is due to a ruptured Graafian follicle, can mimic acute appendicitis, and is managed with explanation, reassurance, simple analgesics and hot-water-bottle comfort.
Bowel obstruction (colicky central pain + vomiting + distension) is among the structured GI differentials screened before settling on a benign gynaecological cause.

The systematic clinical examination and assessment approach (retaining liver/gallbladder questions despite an RLQ site, structured pelvic assessment) reflects the Australian standard method taught in Talley & O'Connor.
citations.source: Nicholas J Talley, Simon O'Connor - Talley and O'Connor's Clinical Examination (8th edition) (p.1)
